message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
A 2.4 × 1.8 m floor is a good size for a first go. It's only 24 tiles, so it's very manageable. Here are your questions in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits slightly higher than the tile next to it. You can feel the ridge with your foot and see it as a thin shadow line when light comes across the floor. A little is normal; too much looks shoddy and can catch toes or a mop.

It's worth knowing about with your tiles in particular. Long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed along their length. If you lay them in a half-and-half brick pattern, the high middle of one tile lines up with the low ends of its neighbours. That's why the usual advice for 60 cm tiles is to offset each row by no more than a third of a tile. Tile levelling clips, sold in packs at tile shops, also help a lot.

## Grout colour

Go a shade or two **darker** than the tile: a mid-grey, not white or very pale grey. Floor grout picks up dirt from footfall and mopping, and pale grout shows it within weeks, which is exactly what you want to avoid. Mid-grey hides it and looks tidy with pale grey porcelain.

Two extra tips:
- **Look at a dried sample.** Grout dries lighter than it looks wet, so check a sample card or a test piece before deciding.
- **Consider stain-resistant grout.** Many brands sell "anti-stain" or epoxy-type grouts. If you use ordinary cement grout, seal it once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tile the whole floor, then fit the toilet on top. You avoid fiddly cuts around the base, the edge looks neater, and if you change the toilet later there's no untiled patch.

## How many boxes

**4 boxes.**
- Floor: 2.4 × 1.8 = 4.32 m²
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need exactly 24 tiles with no waste
- Adding 10% gives 26.4, which rounds up to 27 tiles
- 3 boxes is only 24 tiles, so you need 4 boxes (32 tiles)

The 8 spares are not too many. A third-offset pattern produces cut pieces at the end of each row, and you'll need cuts around the toilet waste pipe and door frame. Real walls are rarely perfectly square either. Keep any leftover tiles: if one ever cracks, you'll have an exact match.

When buying, check that all 4 boxes have the **same batch number**, because shades can vary between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting floor tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from about [9am] to [12pm]. We'll keep it to the morning as far as we can.
>
> Thank you as well for putting up with the skip on the drive for the past couple of weeks. We really appreciate your patience, and it should all be done soon.
>
> If anything's a problem, just give us a knock.
>
> [Your names]

## Three beginner tips

1. **Check the floor before anything else.** It needs to be firm and flat. Lay a long straight edge or spirit level across it in several directions and look for gaps underneath. Tiles copy every dip and bump below them, and a floor that flexes, such as a bouncy timber one, will crack tiles and grout. Fixing the base is the part the videos skip, and it matters most.
2. **Dry-lay the whole floor before mixing any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers and move the layout around. Aim for no thin slivers of tile at the doorway or along the most visible wall. Ten minutes of planning here saves most of the regret later.
3. **Mix adhesive in small batches, and lift a tile early to check.** Adhesive starts to set, so only mix what you can use in about 20–30 minutes. After laying your first few tiles, pull one up and look at the back. It should be almost fully covered. If it isn't, spread adhesive on the back of each tile as well as on the floor ("back-buttering"); this is normal practice for large tiles. Hollow spots under tiles are a common cause of cracking.

After that, keep off the floor for at least 24 hours before grouting, or as long as your adhesive's instructions say.
